turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you are getting into roses, and I can absolutely break this down simply.

Think of your choices in a few big buckets:

Shape and size of the rose
Shrub / bush roses: Round, full plants that make nice bushes. Great for borders, hedges, or mixed beds. Good “all-purpose” choice for beginners.
Climbing roses: Tall, flexible canes that need support like an arch, trellis, fence, or railing. Perfect if you want roses growing up and over something.
Groundcover / landscape roses: Low and spreading. Good for covering a slope, the front of a bed, or filling in space.
Compact / small roses: Stay smaller and work well near walkways, smaller beds, or large containers.
How you want to use the flowers
Cut-flower / long-stem types (often hybrid teas): Fewer blooms at once, but big, classic “florist-style” flowers on long stems that are great for vases.
Masses of blooms for color (floribundas, many shrubs): Lots of flowers at once, often in clusters. These make the whole plant look colorful from a distance.
Bloom style
Repeat blooming: Flowers in waves all season with rest breaks between.
Continuous blooming: Keeps putting out flowers most of the season with only short pauses.
Fragrance level
Strong fragrance: Great if you want that classic rose smell when you walk by.
Light or no fragrance: Often chosen if someone is sensitive to scents, or just prefers the look over the smell.
Sun and space
Full sun (6+ hours): Most roses are happiest here and bloom their best.
Partial shade (about 4 hours): Some roses can still do well, but they will bloom less than in full sun.

A couple of quick notes about what we sell:

All our roses are own-root (grown on their own roots, not grafted) and come in 1-gallon containers with soil.
They are meant to be grown outdoors only; they need winter rest to stay healthy long term.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. A few basics make starting way easier.

1) Soil amendments (optional but very helpful)
These improve your soil so the rose can root and grow well. You don’t have to use them, but they give beginners a nice head start:

Bone meal – Supports strong root development.
Cow manure – Adds long-lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost – Loosens and aerates soil and can also be used as a top layer to help protect roots and keep moisture in.
Worm castings – Gentle, rich nutrients and improved soil structure.

You can mix these into the planting hole and/or use a light layer on top of the soil after planting.

2) Fertilizer (this one is important)
Fertilizing is necessary to keep roses growing and blooming well.

In the first year, a liquid fertilizer is especially beginner friendly because it is easy for the plant to take up.
We offer:
OmniMeal
Founders Fish Fertilizer
Boost & Bloom
You can also use another rose fertilizer you like; the key is feeding regularly during the growing season and following the label directions.

3) A few simple non-product basics
These don’t cost much but make a big difference:

A sunny spot with at least 6 hours of direct sun for best blooms.
Good watering habits: deep watering at the base of the plant, not frequent little sprinkles.
Knowing when to plant: after your last spring frost or at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
